findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as a literal argument
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell syntax, such as `main; malicious-command`, `exec()` executes it with the application's privileges. The previous `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` implementation passed the value directly to Git without invoking a shell. Using a shell also changes cancellation semantics because the returned process represents the shell rather than Git.

findings.title: [P2] Keep Git as the cancellable child process
findings.body:
`exec` returns the shell process rather than `git` itself. On environments such as Windows, calling `.kill()` on the returned `ChildProcess` during a long-running `git show` terminates only the shell and can leave `git.exe` running. The previous `execFile` implementation directly targeted Git, so cancellation reliably stopped the operation.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as an argument without invoking a shell
findings.body:
`exec` interpolates `branch` into a shell command, so an input such as `HEAD; rm -rf /tmp/example` executes arbitrary commands. The previous `execFile` implementation passed the value directly to Git without shell interpretation.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch name as a literal argument instead of shell input
findings.body:
`exec()` interpolates `branch` into a shell command. Any caller-controlled value such as `main; malicious-command` executes arbitrary commands with the application's privileges. The previous `execFile()` implementation did not invoke a shell.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
